parkinsons-law.name: Parkinson's Law
parkinsons-law.one_line: Work expands to fill the time available for its completion.
parkinsons-law.definition: Parkinson's Law is the observation that a task will swell in perceived importance and complexity to fill whatever time you give it. Coined by Cyril Northcote Parkinson in a 1955 Economist essay and expanded in his 1957 book, it started as a wry remark about bureaucracy but holds up as a genuine productivity principle: the amount of work is far less fixed than the deadline that contains it.
examples: A move-out inspection that could take an afternoon stretches across a week when no cutoff is set.
A one-hour report fills the whole day when the day is all that's available; give it thirty minutes and it still gets done.
A repair estimate 'in progress' for two weeks turns out to need two hours of actual work once a hard deadline lands.
parkinsons-law.why_it_matters: In property management the law shows up wherever a process lacks a tight structure: move-out workflows, estimates and large repairs, and tenant/owner communication cycles all expand to fill loose timelines. Turned around, it becomes a tool: set a deliberately short, firm deadline and the work compresses to fit it. The deadline is the lever, not the workload.

dunning-kruger.name: Dunning-Kruger Effect
dunning-kruger.one_line: The least skilled are often the most confident; real experts tend to doubt themselves.
dunning-kruger.definition: The Dunning-Kruger effect is a cognitive bias in which people with low ability at a task overestimate their competence, because the very skills needed to do the task well are the skills needed to recognise how badly they're doing it. Its mirror image is that genuinely skilled people often underestimate themselves, assuming what they find easy is easy for everyone.
examples: A new employee confident they've 'mastered' a process after one week, missing the failure modes an experienced hand watches for.
A skilled technician who downplays their own expertise because the work feels obvious to them.
The gap between 'I read the manual once' and 'I've handled this a hundred times' — the first person is often louder.
dunning-kruger.why_it_matters: It reframes both overconfidence and impostor feelings as predictable, not personal. On a team it argues for humility checks and real feedback: the loudest certainty isn't evidence of competence, and quiet self-doubt often sits with the most capable people. Pairing newer staff with experienced ones surfaces the blind spots the bias hides.

five-dysfunctions.name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team
five-dysfunctions.one_line: Team failure stacks up from the bottom: no trust, then no conflict, no commitment, no accountability, no results.
five-dysfunctions.definition: Patrick Lencioni's model (from his 2002 book) describes five layered causes of team failure, each enabling the next. 1) Absence of trust — members won't show vulnerability. 2) Fear of conflict — the team settles for artificial harmony instead of honest debate. 3) Lack of commitment — without real debate, no one truly buys in. 4) Avoidance of accountability — uncommitted people won't hold each other to standards. 5) Inattention to results — everyone protects their own status over the shared goal.
examples: A meeting where everyone nods, then relitigates the decision in the hallway — artificial harmony hiding unspoken disagreement.
A missed standard nobody mentions, because calling it out feels like conflict.
Individuals optimising their own numbers while the team's outcome slips.
five-dysfunctions.why_it_matters: Because the dysfunctions build on each other, you fix them bottom-up: trust first. A team that can be vulnerable can argue honestly; honest argument produces real commitment; commitment lets people hold each other accountable; accountability keeps everyone pointed at results. Skip the base and the higher fixes don't hold.

kanban.name: Kanban
kanban.one_line: A visual signal that pulls new work only when the previous work is used up.
kanban.definition: Kanban is Japanese for 'sign board' — the cards Toyota used to signal when parts needed reordering. It's a replenishment system built on pull from the customer rather than push from the producer: you make or order more only when a real signal says the downstream step is ready. That prevents overproduction and keeps inventory and work-in-progress low.
examples: Office supplies reordered when a marker card surfaces, not on a guessed schedule — the card is the signal.
A tenant request board where a new card is pulled only as the current one clears, so nothing piles up unseen.
A two-bin system: when the first bin empties, its tag triggers the reorder while the second bin covers the gap.
kanban.why_it_matters: Kanban makes work visible and paces it to real demand instead of to assumptions. Pulling instead of pushing exposes bottlenecks, caps how much is in flight at once, and ties directly to just-in-time: do the right work, in the right amount, at the right time. Writing the process down 'crystallizes' it so it can be followed and taught rather than living in one person's head.

toyota-problem-solving.name: Problem-Solving (Toyota vs Western)
toyota-problem-solving.one_line: Treat a problem as a deviation from standard to fix, not a person to blame.
toyota-problem-solving.definition: The Toyota view reframes what a 'problem' is. In the traditional Western frame a problem means someone messed up, so people hide problems to avoid blame. In the Toyota frame a problem is simply a deviation from standard — surfaced early, traced to a system cause with the 5 Whys, and used as a chance to improve. 'Five Why's equal One How' (5W=1H): keep asking why until the root cause, then act.
examples: Instead of 'who broke this?', asking 'why did the standard allow this to happen?' — and getting a fix that prevents recurrence.
Calling attention to a problem early for help, rather than solving it quietly and letting it recur elsewhere.
Five Whys on a late estimate: late → waited on parts → parts not ordered → no reorder signal → no kanban. Fix the signal, not the person.
toyota-problem-solving.why_it_matters: When problems mean blame, they get hidden, and hidden problems repeat. When problems mean 'deviation from standard', they get surfaced and solved at the root. This is the cultural base under kanban, continuous improvement, and the whole value stream — errors become opportunities for learning rather than occasions for punishment.

pareto-principle.name: Pareto Principle (80/20)
pareto-principle.one_line: Roughly 80% of results come from 20% of the effort or causes.
pareto-principle.definition: The Pareto Principle, or 80/20 rule, observes that outcomes are usually driven by a small share of inputs: a minority of causes, clients, or tasks account for the majority of results. Named after economist Vilfredo Pareto, it's a rule of thumb about imbalance, not an exact law — the split might be 70/30 or 90/10, but the point stands that effort and impact are rarely evenly matched.
examples: A small share of properties or tenants generating most of the workload — or most of the revenue.
A handful of recurring issues causing the bulk of maintenance calls.
Twenty percent of a to-do list delivering most of the day's real value.
pareto-principle.why_it_matters: It's a prioritisation lens. If a fifth of the work drives most of the result, finding and protecting that fifth beats spreading effort evenly. Paired with Parkinson's Law — cut the time, find the vital few — it's a strong argument for focus over busyness.

continuous-improvement.name: Continuous Improvement (CANEI / Kaizen)
continuous-improvement.one_line: Continuous And Never-Ending Improvement — many small gains, forever.
continuous-improvement.definition: Continuous improvement is the discipline of getting a little better constantly rather than waiting for big overhauls. The binder frames it as CANEI — Continuous And Never-Ending Improvement — the local cousin of the Japanese kaizen and of Deming's PDCA cycle (Plan, Do, Check, Act). Improvement never ends; writing each gain down crystallizes it so it can be repeated and taught.
examples: A weekly tweak to a move-out checklist that compounds into a much smoother process over a year.
Running Plan-Do-Check-Act on a communication script: try it, measure, adjust, standardise.
Capturing a fix in writing so the next person inherits the improvement instead of rediscovering it.
continuous-improvement.why_it_matters: Small, steady, documented gains outperform occasional big pushes, because they stick and they teach. It's the engine that turns problem-solving and kanban into a habit rather than a one-off, and it depends on the Toyota view that surfacing problems is good.

bounce-back.name: Bounce Back Initiative
bounce-back.one_line: A method to move forward and resolve when procedures slip.
bounce-back.definition: The Bounce Back Initiative is the binder's own framework for recovering when something goes wrong — when a procedure is missed, a deadline slips, or an agreed task isn't completed. Rather than dwelling on the lapse, it's a structured way to re-engage, resolve the issue, and get the workflow moving again, so a single miss doesn't cascade into lost trust among co-workers.
examples: A missed deadline met with a resolve-and-recover step instead of blame — the team bounces back rather than stalls.
A skipped procedure caught and corrected through a set recovery routine.
Re-establishing momentum after a dropped task so co-workers don't lose confidence.
bounce-back.why_it_matters: Every team slips sometimes; what separates strong teams is how fast and cleanly they recover. Bounce Back ties directly to accountability and trust: a reliable recovery method means a lapse costs the team a moment, not a relationship.

peter-principle.name: Peter Principle
peter-principle.one_line: People rise to their level of incompetence — and stay there.
peter-principle.definition: Laurence J. Peter's 1969 observation that in a hierarchy, employees are promoted for being good at their current job until they land in a role they can't do well — and promotions stop, leaving them stuck there. Over time, positions tend to be filled by people operating at the edge of their competence.
examples: A great property manager promoted into a supervisor role that needs skills nobody trained them for.
Promoting the best technician to office manager and losing a great technician while gaining a struggling manager.
peter-principle.why_it_matters: Promotion should follow demonstrated ability for the NEXT job, not just results in the current one — and staying excellent in a role you love is a valid career path, not a failure.

shut-up-and-listen.name: Shut Up and Listen! (Tilman Fertitta)
shut-up-and-listen.one_line: Billionaire restaurateur Tilman Fertitta's blunt lessons on hospitality, numbers, and leading through change.
shut-up-and-listen.definition: A chapter-by-chapter scan of Tilman Fertitta's 2019 book Shut Up and Listen! — hard business truths from the owner of Landry's and the Houston Rockets. The selected spreads cover hospitality ('the plussing culture'), never saying no to a customer, catering to the masses not the classes, knowing your numbers cold, the 'the 5%' rule (it's the 5 percent you don't control that hurts you), cash flow, keeping your hands dirty, teaching one-on-one, anticipating change, hiring people stronger than you, and never giving up.
examples: 'Never say no' — find a way to accommodate the customer even when the first answer is no.
Know your numbers: if you can't state your occupancy, delinquency, and cash position from memory, you're not running the business.
The 5%: obsess over the small fraction of details that can sink you.
shut-up-and-listen.why_it_matters: OPM is a hospitality business as much as a property business — owners and tenants judge us the way diners judge a restaurant. These pages are the binder's core customer-service and numbers curriculum.

'Time creates money' — buying back your hours by handing work to the right who.
who-not-how.why_it_matters: It reframes delegation from a luxury into the main engine of growth — directly applicable to how OPM splits work between staff, vendors, and systems.
